title: Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors and Positive Definite Matrices
description: Eigenvalues and diagonalization, the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, quadratic forms, positive definite matrices and power iteration.
overview: Most matrices turn most vectors into vectors pointing elsewhere. An eigenvector is a direction that the matrix leaves unchanged, apart from stretching: Av = λv. Along such directions the matrix acts as a simple number, and a matrix that has enough of them can be understood completely as independent stretches along different axes.

Eigenvalues determine whether an iteration converges (a Markov chain, gradient descent, a recurrent network), how curved a loss surface is in each direction (the Hessian), and which directions carry the most variance (PCA). Symmetric matrices, which are the common case in machine learning, have especially clean eigenstructure.
objectives: Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a small matrix from the characteristic polynomial.
Diagonalize a matrix, and use A = PDP⁻¹ to compute powers and to analyze iterations.
State the spectral theorem and use A = QΛQᵀ for symmetric matrices.
Test whether a symmetric matrix is positive definite, and relate this to quadratic forms, covariance matrices and Hessians.
Use the Rayleigh quotient, the condition number and power iteration.

sections.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
terms: eigenvalues, eigenvectors and positive definite matrices
body: Most matrices rotate and stretch vectors in complicated ways. But often there are special directions along which the matrix does something very simple: it only stretches or shrinks, and the vector stays on the same line. For A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], the vector (1, 1) becomes (3, 3): same direction, three times as long. The direction (1, 1) is an eigenvector, and the stretch factor 3 is its eigenvalue. A non-zero vector v is an **eigenvector** of the square matrix A with **eigenvalue** λ if

Rewrite as (A − λI)v = 0. A non-zero solution exists only if A − λI is singular, so the eigenvalues are the roots of the **characteristic polynomial** det(A − λI) = 0. For each eigenvalue, the eigenvectors are the non-zero vectors of the null space of A − λI. For a 2 × 2 matrix the polynomial is λ² − (tr A)λ + det A. In general, tr A = Σλ_i and det A = Πλ_i.

example.title: Eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 matrix
example.problem: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]].
solution: tr A = 4, det A = 3, so λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0 and λ = 3 or 1.
Check: A(1, 1) = (3, 3) = 3(1, 1) ✓ and A(1, −1) = (1, −1) ✓. The eigenvalues satisfy 3 + 1 = tr A and 3 · 1 = det A.

list: A real matrix can have complex eigenvalues. The rotation by 90°, [[0, −1], [1, 0]], has characteristic polynomial λ² + 1 = 0 and eigenvalues ±i: no real direction is preserved. Complex eigenvalues of a real matrix come in conjugate pairs and describe rotation combined with scaling; their magnitude controls growth.
The eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal entries.
A is singular exactly when 0 is an eigenvalue.
Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.

sections.title: Diagonalization and powers
body: Why bother? Because applying a matrix many times is easy along its special directions: an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3 is multiplied by 3, then 9, then 27, while one with eigenvalue 0.5 shrinks to half, a quarter and an eighth. Any vector can be split into its pieces along the eigenvectors, and each piece grows or shrinks on its own. After many steps the piece with the largest eigenvalue dominates. If A has n linearly independent eigenvectors, put them in the columns of P and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of D. Then AP = PD, so
A is then **diagonalizable**: in the basis of its eigenvectors it is the diagonal matrix D (see Change of basis). Powers become easy:

To compute Aᵏx, expand x = c₁v₁ + … + c_nv_n in the eigenvectors; then Aᵏx = c₁λ₁ᵏv₁ + … + c_nλ_nᵏv_n. The behavior of a repeated map is controlled by the eigenvalues: if all |λ_i| < 1 then Aᵏx → 0; if one has |λ| > 1 the iteration blows up along its eigenvector, and the eigenvalue of largest magnitude dominates for large k. The largest magnitude is the **spectral radius**.

example.title: A Markov chain
example.problem: A user is either active or inactive. Each day an active user stays active with probability 0.9, and an inactive user becomes active with probability 0.5. Find the long-run fraction of active days.
solution: The state distribution evolves by p ← Tp with T = [[0.9, 0.5], [0.1, 0.5]] (each column sums to 1).
tr T = 1.4 and det T = 0.45 − 0.05 = 0.4, so λ² − 1.4λ + 0.4 = 0 gives λ = 1 and 0.4.

The component along the λ = 0.4 eigenvector decays like 0.4ᵏ; what survives is the λ = 1 eigenvector, the stationary distribution: (T − I)p = 0 gives −0.1p₁ + 0.5p₂ = 0, so p₁ = 5p₂, and with p₁ + p₂ = 1, p = (5/6, 1/6). In the long run a user is active 83% of the time, whatever the start. The error shrinks by 0.4 per step.

example.title: Gradient descent seen through eigenvalues
example.problem: Minimize f(x) = ½xᵀHx with H having eigenvalues 10 and 1. The update is x ← (I − αH)x. What is the largest stable α, and the best α?
example.solution: In the eigenbasis the error components shrink by |1 − αλ| with λ = 10 and 1. Stability needs |1 − 10α| < 1, so α < 0.2. The best α balances the two: 1 − α = −(1 − 10α), i.e. α = 2/11 = 0.182, giving factors ±0.818 per step. The convergence rate is (κ − 1)/(κ + 1) with condition number κ = 10.

body.warn: Not every matrix is diagonalizable. [[1, 1], [0, 1]] has the repeated eigenvalue 1 and only one independent eigenvector (1, 0): it is **defective**. Its powers grow linearly, [[1, k], [0, 1]], which diagonal matrices cannot produce. Symmetric matrices are never defective.

sections.title: The spectral theorem
body: Symmetric matrices (Aᵀ = A) are the matrices of covariances, Gram matrices, Hessians and AᵀA, and they have the best possible eigenstructure.

body.key: Spectral theorem. A real symmetric n × n matrix has real eigenvalues, and has n orthonormal eigenvectors. It can be written A = QΛQᵀ, with Q orthogonal (its columns are the eigenvectors) and Λ = diag(λ₁, …, λ_n).

body: Equivalently, A = Σ_i λ_i q_iq_iᵀ: a sum of rank-one projections, each scaled by an eigenvalue. Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are automatically orthogonal. **Proof sketch** of this orthogonality: if Av = λv and Aw = μw with λ ≠ μ, then λ(vᵀw) = (Av)ᵀw = vᵀAᵀw = vᵀAw = μ(vᵀw), so (λ − μ)vᵀw = 0 and vᵀw = 0.

example.title: Spectral decomposition
example.solution: The eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, −1) are orthogonal; normalize them: q₁ = (1, 1)/√2, q₂ = (1, −1)/√2. Then A = 3q₁q₁ᵀ + 1q₂q₂ᵀ = 3 · ½[[1, 1], [1, 1]] + ½[[1, −1], [−1, 1]] = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] ✓.

body: Consequences: the inverse is A⁻¹ = QΛ⁻¹Qᵀ, a power is Aᵏ = QΛᵏQᵀ, and a function f(A) = Qf(Λ)Qᵀ (such as the matrix exponential or square root). The determinant is Πλ_i, and the operator norm ‖A‖₂ = max|λ_i|. For PCA, the covariance matrix is diagonalized and the principal components are its eigenvectors.

sections.title: Quadratic forms and positive definite matrices
body: The simplest bowl is f(x, y) = x² + y²: it curves upward in every direction and has one lowest point. By contrast f(x, y) = x² − y² curves up along x but down along y, like a saddle. Positive definite matrices are exactly the ones whose quadratic form is a bowl. That matters for optimization: a bowl has a single minimum that gradient descent finds. A **quadratic form** is the scalar xᵀAx for a symmetric A. It is how the curvature of a loss, the variance of a projection and the squared length in a weighted norm are written. A symmetric matrix is **positive definite** (PD) if xᵀAx > 0 for every x ≠ 0, and **positive semidefinite** (PSD) if xᵀAx ≥ 0.

list: **Eigenvalue test**: A is PD iff all eigenvalues are > 0, and PSD iff all are ≥ 0. (In the eigenbasis, xᵀAx = Σλ_ic_i².)
**Pivot / minor test**: A is PD iff all leading principal minors (the determinants of the top-left 1 × 1, 2 × 2, … blocks) are positive.
**Cholesky**: A is PD iff A = LLᵀ for an invertible lower triangular L.
**Gram matrices**: for any matrix B, BᵀB is PSD, because xᵀBᵀBx = ‖Bx‖² ≥ 0; it is PD iff B has independent columns. Covariance matrices and the Hessian of least squares are of this kind.

example.title: Testing definiteness
example.solution: First: the minors are 2 and 4 − 1 = 3, both positive, so it is PD (eigenvalues 1 and 3). Second: det = 1 − 4 = −3 < 0, so one eigenvalue is negative: its eigenvalues are 3 and −1 and the matrix is indefinite. The form is negative along (1, −1): xᵀAx = 1 + 1 − 4 = −2.

body: For a PD matrix A the set {x : xᵀAx = 1} is an ellipsoid whose axes point along the eigenvectors, with semi-axis lengths 1/√λ_i. The **Rayleigh quotient** R(x) = xᵀAx/xᵀx lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalues, attaining them at the corresponding eigenvectors:
So maximizing the variance uᵀΣu of a projection over unit vectors gives the top eigenvector of Σ: this is PCA.

The **condition number** of a PD matrix is κ = λ_max/λ_min. It measures how elongated the ellipsoid is, how much the solution of Ax = b can be amplified by errors in b (relative error up to κ times larger), and how slowly gradient descent converges on ½xᵀAx (the rate is (κ − 1)/(κ + 1)). A matrix is ill-conditioned when κ is large.

example.title: Convergence rate from the condition number
example.problem: A quadratic has Hessian eigenvalues 100 and 1. How fast does gradient descent with the best fixed step converge, and how many steps reduce the error by a factor of 1000?
example.solution: κ = 100, so the factor per step is (100 − 1)/(100 + 1) = 0.9802. Then 0.9802ⁿ = 10⁻³ gives n = ln(1000)/(−ln 0.9802) = 6.908/0.02 = 345 steps. With κ = 1 (a perfectly round bowl) one step would suffice.

sections.title: Computing eigenvalues: power iteration and applications
body: Eigenvalues are not found in practice from the characteristic polynomial (its roots are extremely sensitive to errors, and it cannot be solved in closed form beyond degree 4). The **QR algorithm** (iterated QR factorizations) is the standard dense method and costs O(n³). For the top eigenvector of a huge sparse matrix, use **power iteration**: repeatedly apply A and normalize,
Expanding x₀ in the eigenvectors, Aᵏx₀ is dominated by the term with the largest |λ|, so x_k converges to the dominant eigenvector at rate |λ₂/λ₁|. The Rayleigh quotient estimates the eigenvalue.

example.title: Power iteration
example.problem: Apply power iteration to A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] from x₀ = (1, 0), without normalizing, for three steps.
example.solution: x₁ = (2, 1), x₂ = A(2, 1) = (5, 4), x₃ = A(5, 4) = (14, 13). The direction approaches (1, 1). The Rayleigh quotient at x₂ is (5, 4)·(14, 13)/41 = 122/41 = 2.976, close to the dominant eigenvalue 3. The error shrinks by |λ₂/λ₁| = 1/3 per step.

list: **PageRank**: the importance of web pages is the stationary distribution (the dominant eigenvector, with λ = 1) of a Markov chain that follows random links, computed by power iteration on a matrix with billions of rows.
**PCA and the SVD**: eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (see the next chapter for the SVD).
**Spectral clustering**: eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian (see Clustering).
**Stability of recurrent networks**: the largest singular value of the recurrent weight matrix decides whether gradients vanish or explode (see Sequence Models).
**Optimization**: the Hessian's eigenvalues give the curvature in each direction, the largest stable learning rate 2/λ_max and the condition number.

check.a: the eigenvector with the largest-magnitude eigenvalue
wrong: the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue

quiz.q: What are the eigenvalues of A = [[1, 4], [2, 3]]?
quiz.why: tr A = 4 and det A = 3 − 8 = −5, so λ² − 4λ − 5 = (λ − 5)(λ + 1) = 0. The pair 4 and −5 mixes up the trace and determinant with the roots.

quiz.q: A real 2 × 2 matrix has the eigenvalue 1 + 2i. What is its other eigenvalue?
quiz.why: Complex eigenvalues of a real matrix come in conjugate pairs, because the characteristic polynomial has real coefficients. The magnitude √5 > 1 means repeated application grows vectors.

quiz.q: A 3 × 3 matrix has trace 9, and two of its eigenvalues are 2 and 3. What is its determinant?
quiz.why: The eigenvalues sum to the trace, so the third is 9 − 5 = 4. The determinant is the product 2 · 3 · 4 = 24.

quiz.q: A has eigenvalues 2 and −1. What are the eigenvalues of A⁶?
quiz.why: If Av = λv then A⁶v = λ⁶v. Here 2⁶ = 64 and (−1)⁶ = 1; an even power removes the sign.

quiz.q: x ← Ax is iterated from a generic start. Which set of eigenvalues makes the iteration diverge?
quiz.why: Divergence needs a magnitude above 1, and |−1.1| > 1. The complex pair has magnitude √(0.64 + 0.25) ≈ 0.94, which is below 1, so it shrinks despite the large real part.

quiz.q: On sunny days the weather stays sunny with probability 0.8, and a rainy day turns sunny with probability 0.3. With T = [[0.8, 0.3], [0.2, 0.7]] and p ← Tp, what is the long-run (sunny, rainy) distribution?
quiz.why: The stationary vector solves (T − I)p = 0, which gives −0.2p₁ + 0.3p₂ = 0, so p₁ = 1.5p₂ and with p₁ + p₂ = 1, p = (0.6, 0.4). It is the eigenvector for λ = 1.

quiz.q: Gradient descent on a quadratic with Hessian eigenvalues 4 and 1 uses the best fixed step size. What is it?
quiz.why: Balance the two shrink factors: 1 − α = −(1 − 4α) gives α = 2/5 = 0.4, with factor ±0.6 per step. The step 0.5 equals 2/λ_max and is only the stability limit, where one component neither grows nor shrinks.

quiz.a: The repeated eigenvalue 3 has only one independent eigenvector
quiz.why: A − 3I = [[0, 1], [0, 0]] has a one-dimensional null space, so there are not 2 independent eigenvectors. Non-symmetric matrices with distinct eigenvalues can still be diagonalized.

quiz.q: What is the operator norm ‖A‖₂ of the symmetric matrix A = [[−1, 2], [2, −1]]?
quiz.why: Its eigenvalues are 1 and −3 (trace −2, determinant −3). For a symmetric matrix ‖A‖₂ = max|λ_i| = 3, so the sign is irrelevant and the largest eigenvalue 1 is not the answer.

quiz.q: Which matrix is guaranteed to have an orthonormal set of eigenvectors?
quiz.a: BᵀB for any real matrix B
wrong: [[1, 1], [0, 2]], since its eigenvalues are real and distinct
quiz.why: BᵀB is symmetric, so the spectral theorem applies. The matrix [[1, 1], [0, 2]] has eigenvectors (1, 0) and (1, 1), which are not orthogonal.

quiz.q: A = 10 q₁q₁ᵀ with q₁ = (0.6, 0.8). What is the entry in row 1, column 2 of A?
quiz.why: (q₁q₁ᵀ)₁₂ = 0.6 × 0.8 = 0.48, and multiplying by the eigenvalue 10 gives 4.8. A is a rank-one matrix with eigenvalue 10 along q₁ and 0 otherwise.

quiz.q: For which values of k is [[2, k], [k, 8]] positive definite?
quiz.why: The minors are 2 and 16 − k², so we need k² < 16. At k = ±4 the determinant is 0 and the matrix is only semidefinite. Negative k works equally, since only k² appears.

quiz.q: What is the Rayleigh quotient xᵀAx/xᵀx of A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]] at x = (1, −1)?
quiz.why: xᵀAx = 3 and xᵀx = 2, so the quotient is 1.5, between the eigenvalues 1.38 and 3.62. The value 3 forgets to divide by xᵀx.

quiz.q: A is positive definite with eigenvalues 4 and 25. What are the semi-axis lengths of the ellipse {x : xᵀAx = 1}?
quiz.why: The semi-axis along an eigenvector is 1/√λ, so 1/2 and 1/5. Large eigenvalues (steep curvature) give short axes.

quiz.q: A data matrix X has a third column equal to the sum of its first two columns. What is true of XᵀX?
quiz.a: It is positive semidefinite and singular
quiz.why: XᵀX is always symmetric and PSD, since vᵀXᵀXv = ‖Xv‖² ≥ 0. With dependent columns some v ≠ 0 has Xv = 0, so 0 is an eigenvalue and XᵀX is not PD.

quiz.q: Gradient descent with the best fixed step runs on a quadratic with Hessian eigenvalues 9 and 1. After 10 steps, the error is multiplied by about
quiz.why: The factor per step is (κ − 1)/(κ + 1) = 8/10 = 0.8, and 0.8¹⁰ ≈ 0.107. Using (κ − 1)/κ ≈ 0.89 would give 0.35.

quiz.q: Power iteration without normalization is applied to A = [[1, 2], [2, 1]], starting from (1, 0). What is the vector after two steps?
quiz.why: The first step gives A(1, 0) = (1, 2) and the second gives A(1, 2) = (1 + 4, 2 + 2) = (5, 4). The direction is moving toward (1, 1), the dominant eigenvector for λ = 3.

summary: Av = λv. Eigenvalues are the roots of det(A − λI) = 0; their sum is the trace and their product is the determinant.

A diagonalizable matrix is A = PDP⁻¹, so Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹. Iterations converge when the spectral radius is below 1, at a rate set by the second-largest eigenvalue. Stationary distributions of Markov chains are eigenvectors with λ = 1.
Spectral theorem: a real symmetric matrix is A = QΛQᵀ with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors.

A symmetric matrix is positive definite iff all eigenvalues are positive (equivalently, positive leading minors or A = LLᵀ). BᵀB is PSD. The Rayleigh quotient lies between λ_min and λ_max, which gives PCA. The condition number κ = λ_max/λ_min governs gradient descent and error amplification.
Compute top eigenvectors by power iteration; dense eigenproblems use the QR algorithm.

problems.q: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]].
For A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], compute A⁵ using the eigendecomposition.
Is [[4, 2], [2, 1]] positive definite or semidefinite? Give its eigenvalues.
problems.solution: det = 4 − 4 = 0 and trace 5, so the eigenvalues are 5 and 0. It is positive semidefinite but not definite. Indeed xᵀAx = (2x₁ + x₂)² vanishes along (1, −2).

problems.q: A Hessian has eigenvalues 0.01, 1 and 50. Find the condition number, the largest stable learning rate, and the rate per step with the optimal fixed step.
problems.solution: κ = 50/0.01 = 5000. Stability needs α < 2/50 = 0.04. The best fixed step gives a factor (κ − 1)/(κ + 1) = 4999/5001 = 0.9996 per step, so hundreds of thousands of steps would be needed: the problem is badly conditioned and needs preconditioning or a second-order method.

problems.q: Show that the eigenvalues of a positive semidefinite matrix are non-negative.
problems.solution: If Av = λv with ‖v‖ = 1 then λ = vᵀAv ≥ 0 by positive semidefiniteness.
